likert_scale.label: Learner
likert_scale.meaning: Just getting started. Needs guidance to apply this.

likert_scale.label: Developing
likert_scale.meaning: Building awareness. Can do this with support but not yet independently.

likert_scale.label: Advanced
likert_scale.meaning: Goes beyond the basics. Others notice and benefit from their strength here.

likert_scale.label: Expert
likert_scale.meaning: Genuine mastery. Others come to them for this. Raising the bar for the team.

competencies.name: Business Sense
competencies.what_it_covers: Understanding how the business works, what success looks like commercially, and how design decisions connect to business outcomes.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time a design decision you made was directly connected to a business outcome -- revenue, retention, conversion, cost. What was the connection?
designer.opening_probe: How did you know the design was the lever? What would have happened if you'd made a different call?

follow_threads.question: How do you typically stay connected to what the business is trying to achieve? Is that information coming to you, or are you going to get it?
follow_threads.probe: Has your understanding of the business ever changed how you approached a design problem? What shifted?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a design request because you thought it was the wrong call for the business -- even if it was what a stakeholder wanted.
follow_threads.probe: How did you make that case? Did it land?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 scale for business sense -- understanding how your design work connects to how the business actually works and what it's trying to achieve?

1 means you're still building that picture. 5 means you're regularly making design decisions with a clear view of the commercial implications and others come to you for that perspective.

manager.opening_prompt: Can you point to a moment where this designer's understanding of the business -- or lack of it -- directly affected a design outcome?
manager.opening_probe: Was it a positive or negative impact? Did they recognize the connection themselves?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer stay connected to what the business is trying to achieve? Do they seek that context out, or do they wait for it to come to them?
follow_threads.probe: Have they ever surprised you with business knowledge you didn't expect them to have?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever pushed back on a request on business grounds -- not just design grounds? What happened?
follow_threads.probe: Were they right? How did the team receive it?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 scale for business sense?

1 means they're still building a picture of how the business works. 5 means they regularly connect design decisions to commercial outcomes and others trust their read on the business.

competencies.name: Engineering Understanding
competencies.what_it_covers: Working mental model of the technical environment, feasibility awareness, and designing for how things are actually built.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a design decision you made that required you to understand something about how the product was actually built. What did you need to learn and how did you learn it?
designer.opening_probe: Did your understanding of the constraints change your design? How?

follow_threads.question: How would the engineers you've worked with describe you as a collaborator? Be honest.
follow_threads.probe: Is there something specific you've gotten better at? Something you're still working on?

follow_threads.question: Have you designed for a product or feature that involved AI -- recommendations, predictions, generated content? What did you need to understand about how the system worked to design it well?
follow_threads.probe: Did you design for what happens when it gets it wrong? How did you think about that?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 scale for engineering understanding?

1 means you rely heavily on engineers to tell you what's possible. 5 means you have a strong working mental model and engineers trust that your designs are buildable.

manager.opening_prompt: How well does this designer understand the technical environment they design for? Do they have a working mental model, or do they need a lot of support from engineering to understand what's feasible?
manager.opening_probe: Have you had to intervene because a design wasn't technically grounded?

follow_threads.question: How would you describe this designer's relationship with the engineers they work with? Do engineers trust their work?
follow_threads.probe: Have engineers ever come to you with concerns about buildability? Do they collaborate during implementation or hand off and disappear?

follow_threads.question: If this designer has worked on AI-powered features, how did they approach understanding the underlying system? Did they design for edge cases and failure states?
follow_threads.probe: Did they treat it as a black box or did they ask questions about how it behaves?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for engineering understanding?

1 means heavy reliance on engineering to define feasibility. 5 means strong technical mental model, builds well, engineers trust the work.

competencies.name: Domain Knowledge
competencies.what_it_covers: Depth of understanding of the problem space, user context, and industry-specific nuance.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a design decision you made that a designer without your domain knowledge would have gotten wrong. What did you know that made the difference?
designer.opening_probe: How did you acquire that knowledge? Was it deliberate or did it accumulate over time?

follow_threads.question: How do you stay current with what's happening in the space you design for? What's your actual routine?
follow_threads.probe: Has something you learned recently changed how you think about your users? What shifted?

follow_threads.question: Have you ever designed for a space where getting the domain wrong -- regulations, compliance, safety, legal -- could have caused real harm? How did you handle that?
follow_threads.probe: Where did you go to verify you had it right? Did AI play any role, and how did you treat what it told you?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for domain knowledge in the spaces you design for?

1 means you're still building basic familiarity. 5 means deep expertise -- you're the person others come to for context on the problem space.

manager.opening_prompt: Has this designer ever made a call that required real domain knowledge -- something a designer from outside the space might have gotten wrong?
manager.opening_probe: How did you know the call was right? Did they have to advocate for it, or did the team trust their read?

follow_threads.question: Does this designer actively stay current with what's happening in the space they design for? How do you know?
follow_threads.probe: Have they ever brought something new to the team from their own learning? Do they challenge assumptions about users or the market?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer worked on anything where regulatory, compliance, or safety considerations were in play? How did they handle the responsibility?
follow_threads.probe: Did they know to escalate or verify, or did they treat it like any other design problem? Did you have to intervene?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for domain knowledge?

1 means still building basic familiarity. 5 means deep expertise the team relies on.

competencies.name: Established UX Conventions
competencies.what_it_covers: Understanding of interaction patterns, platform conventions, accessibility standards, and when to follow vs. break them intentionally.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time you had to decide whether to follow an established UX convention or break from it. What was the call and how did you make it?
designer.opening_probe: What would have been lost by following the convention? What would have been lost by breaking it?

follow_threads.question: How do you keep your knowledge of platform conventions and accessibility standards current? What's your actual practice?
follow_threads.probe: Has a convention or standard you learned recently changed how you approach something you'd been doing a certain way?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time someone on your team or a stakeholder pushed for something that violated a UX convention in a way that would have hurt the user. What did you do?
follow_threads.probe: How did you make the case? Did it change the outcome?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for established UX conventions?

1 means you're still building awareness of the conventions that apply to your work. 5 means deep fluency -- you know the rules well enough to know exactly when and why to break them.

manager.opening_prompt: How well does this designer understand and apply UX conventions, platform patterns, and accessibility standards? Can you give me an example either way?
manager.opening_probe: Have you ever had to flag a convention violation in their work? How did they respond?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever made a strong case for following -- or deliberately breaking -- a convention? What was the situation?
follow_threads.probe: Were they right? How did the team receive their reasoning?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer handle situations where a stakeholder or teammate pushes for something that would hurt the user experience based on convention or accessibility?
follow_threads.probe: Do they defer, or do they advocate? Can they back it up with reasoning?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for established UX conventions?

1 means still building awareness. 5 means deep fluency, knows when and why to follow or break conventions, and can make the case clearly.

competencies.name: Systems Thinking
competencies.what_it_covers: Ability to see patterns, design at scale, create reusable solutions, and understand how components interact across a product.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time you identified a pattern in a product that was creating problems at scale -- inconsistency, duplication, fragility. What did you do about it?
designer.opening_probe: How did you identify it? Was it obvious to others or did you have to make the case?

follow_threads.question: How do you approach designing something new when you know it needs to work within a larger system? Walk me through how that thinking shows up in your process.
follow_threads.probe: What breaks when designers don't think this way? Have you seen that happen?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a contribution you've made to a design system -- a pattern, a component, a principle. What problem were you solving and what made the solution durable?
follow_threads.probe: Has it held up? Has it been adopted? Has anything broken it?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for systems thinking?

1 means you're primarily focused on individual screens or flows. 5 means you're designing for scale and coherence across the whole product, and others rely on your systems thinking to keep things from fragmenting.

manager.opening_prompt: Can you give me an example of this designer thinking at a systems level -- seeing patterns, designing for reuse, or identifying something that was fragile at scale?
manager.opening_probe: Did they see it themselves or did someone point it out? What did they do with it?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer approach new work in the context of the broader design system? Do they design for fit, or do they design in isolation and figure out the fit later?
follow_threads.probe: Have you had to pull back a design because it wasn't considering the system?

follow_threads.question: What has this designer contributed to your design system? Was it adopted? Has it held up?
follow_threads.probe: How do other designers engage with their contributions?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for systems thinking?

1 means focused on individual screens. 5 means designing for coherence and scale, others rely on them to keep the system together.

competencies.name: Content Strategy
competencies.what_it_covers: UX writing quality, information architecture, how content decisions shape the user experience, and how AI is used in content work.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time the words in a UI significantly changed how users experienced something. What was the content problem and what made the solution work?
designer.opening_probe: How did you arrive at that solution? What did you try that didn't work?

follow_threads.question: How do you approach writing UI copy -- error messages, empty states, CTAs, onboarding? What's your process and how do you know when it's good?
follow_threads.probe: Have you ever used AI to help write or improve copy? What did you do with what it gave you?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time information architecture -- how content was organized and structured -- was the core design problem. How did you approach it?
follow_threads.probe: What made it hard? What would have happened if you'd gotten it wrong?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for content strategy?

1 means content is an afterthought in your process. 5 means you treat content as a core design material -- structure, voice, and clarity are central to how you solve problems.

manager.opening_prompt: How does this designer treat content and copy in their work? Is it something they think about deliberately, or does it feel like a gap?
manager.opening_probe: Can you point to a piece of their work where the content was notably strong or weak?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever led or significantly contributed to an information architecture decision? What was the problem and how did they approach it?
follow_threads.probe: Did they get it right? Did it hold up?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer use AI in content work? Do they direct it with judgment or tend to use what it gives them?
follow_threads.probe: Have you seen output that felt like it came from AI without enough design judgment applied?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for content strategy?

1 means content is rarely considered in their process. 5 means they treat content as core craft, with strong judgment on structure, voice, and clarity.

competencies.name: Qualitative UX Research
competencies.what_it_covers: Planning, conducting, and synthesizing qualitative research, and connecting insights to design decisions.

designer.opening_prompt: Walk me through how you approached a recent research project from start to finish. What did the process actually look like?
designer.opening_probe: How did you decide what counted as a theme versus noise? How did synthesis feel -- rushed, thorough, somewhere in between?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time you caught something in your research that didn't hold up under scrutiny -- yours or someone else's. What happened?
follow_threads.probe: What made you question it? What did you do with that finding?

follow_threads.question: How do you typically share research findings, and how do you know if they actually landed and changed anything?
follow_threads.probe: Can you point to a decision that changed because of research you did? And one that should have but didn't?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for qualitative UX research?

1 means you're still building your research practice. 5 means you're genuinely expert level -- rigorous, influential, others come to you for this.

manager.opening_prompt: Think about research this designer has done in the last six months. Can you point to a decision that changed because of their work?
manager.opening_probe: How do they typically present and share findings? Does the research actually influence decisions or does it get filed away?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time this designer caught something in their research that didn't hold up, or pushed back on a finding that wasn't solid.
follow_threads.probe: Have you ever had to flag a research quality concern to them? How did they respond?

follow_threads.question: How much do they drive the scope and direction of research efforts versus waiting for direction?
follow_threads.probe: Do they come to you with a research plan, or do they wait for one?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for qualitative UX research?

1 means still developing a research practice. 5 means rigorous, independent, influential -- research they do changes decisions.

competencies.name: Interaction Design
competencies.what_it_covers: Depth of interaction thinking, edge case coverage, flow design, and quality of the decision-making that underlies UI work.

designer.opening_prompt: Walk me through a recent interaction design problem that was genuinely hard. What made it hard, and how did you work through it?
designer.opening_probe: What did you try first? What didn't work? How did you know when you had it right?

follow_threads.question: How do you approach edge cases and failure states in your work? Are you designing for them from the start or discovering them later?
follow_threads.probe: Tell me about a time an edge case you hadn't anticipated caused a real problem. What happened?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a piece of interaction design work you'd do differently now. What would you change and why?
follow_threads.probe: What did you know then? What do you know now that you didn't?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for interaction design?

1 means you're still developing fluency with interaction patterns and edge case thinking. 5 means exceptional depth -- others come to you to pressure test their flows and your interaction thinking raises the bar for the team.

manager.opening_prompt: How would you describe the quality of this designer's interaction thinking? Not the visual output -- the decisions underneath it. Edge cases, flows, error states.
manager.opening_probe: Can you point to a piece of their work that shows their interaction design at its best?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever caught an edge case or failure state that others missed? What happened?
follow_threads.probe: Do they tend to find these themselves or do they surface in QA or user testing?

follow_threads.question: Where do you think this designer still has room to grow in their interaction design? Be honest.
follow_threads.probe: Have you had to send work back because the interaction thinking wasn't thorough enough?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for interaction design?

1 means developing fluency. 5 means exceptional depth in interaction thinking, edge cases, and flow design -- raises the bar for the team.

competencies.name: Visual Design
competencies.what_it_covers: Visual craft, aesthetic sensibility, typography, color, hierarchy, and the ability to direct and evaluate visual quality.

designer.opening_prompt: Show me or describe a piece of your visual work you're proud of. What makes it good? Be specific.
designer.opening_probe: What would a less experienced designer have missed? What would you do differently now?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time you had to push back on a visual direction -- yours or someone else's -- because it wasn't working. How did you articulate what was wrong?
follow_threads.probe: Could you name what was wrong, or was it more of a feel? What did you do about it?

follow_threads.question: How do you use AI in your visual work? Where does it show up in your process and how do you evaluate what it produces?
follow_threads.probe: Has AI ever given you something that looked right but felt wrong? What did you do?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for visual design?

1 means visual craft is still a developing area. 5 means strong, confident aesthetic sensibility -- you have a clear point of view and can both produce and direct high-quality visual work.

manager.opening_prompt: How would you describe this designer's visual craft? Where are they strong and where are the gaps?
manager.opening_probe: What's a piece of their work you'd point to as representative of their best visual output?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever pushed back on a visual direction -- theirs or someone else's -- in a way that improved the outcome?
follow_threads.probe: Can they articulate what's wrong with something visually, or do they just have a feeling about it?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer use AI in visual work? Do they direct it with taste and judgment, or do they tend to use what it gives them?
follow_threads.probe: Have you reviewed work where AI output was used without enough critical evaluation?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for visual design?

1 means visual craft is still developing. 5 means strong aesthetic sensibility, clear point of view, can produce and direct high-quality visual work.

competencies.name: Prototyping & Motion Design
competencies.what_it_covers: Ability to prototype ideas at the right fidelity, use motion to communicate interaction, and use prototyping as a thinking and validation tool.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time prototyping changed what you thought was the right design. What did you learn from building it that you wouldn't have learned from a static mock?
designer.opening_probe: At what point in your process do you typically prototype? Has that changed over time?

follow_threads.question: How do you decide what fidelity to prototype at? What factors drive that call?
follow_threads.probe: Tell me about a time you over- or under-prototyped. What happened?

follow_threads.question: How do you use motion and animation in your work? Is it intentional communication or more decorative? Tell me about a specific example.
follow_threads.probe: How did you decide what to animate? How did you know it was helping rather than adding noise?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for prototyping and motion design?

1 means prototyping is still a developing skill and motion is rarely part of your work. 5 means you use prototyping fluidly as a thinking tool and motion is an intentional, well-considered part of how you communicate interaction.

manager.opening_prompt: How does this designer use prototyping in their process? Is it a genuine thinking tool or does it come late as a demonstration?
manager.opening_probe: Can you think of a time prototyping changed the design? Did they initiate it or did someone suggest it?

follow_threads.question: Does this designer make deliberate choices about prototype fidelity, or do they tend to default to one approach?
follow_threads.probe: Have you ever felt they spent too much or too little time prototyping?

follow_threads.question: How does motion and animation show up in their work? Is it intentional or decorative?
follow_threads.probe: Has motion ever been a point of feedback -- positively or negatively -- in their work?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for prototyping and motion design?

1 means prototyping is still developing and motion is rarely considered. 5 means fluent use of prototyping as a thinking tool and intentional, well-calibrated motion design.

competencies.name: Ability to Learn Quickly
competencies.what_it_covers: How fast and accurately someone builds new knowledge, recovers from being wrong, and transfers learning into their work.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time you had to get up to speed on something completely new -- a domain, a tool, a methodology -- quickly. How did you do it and how did you know when you knew enough?
designer.opening_probe: What was the first thing you got wrong about it? How did you find out?

follow_threads.question: How do you use AI to accelerate your own learning? Tell me about a specific case.
follow_threads.probe: How did you verify what it told you? Did you find errors or gaps?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about something you believed six months ago -- about design, about your users, about your domain -- that you've since updated. What changed your mind?
follow_threads.probe: Was it uncomfortable to change that view? What made you willing to?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for ability to learn quickly?

1 means learning is slow or you tend to stay in familiar territory. 5 means you pick up new things fast, verify accurately, and integrate new knowledge into your work visibly and quickly.

manager.opening_prompt: Think about a time this designer had to learn something new quickly -- a new domain, tool, or type of problem. How did they approach it and how accurate was their learning?
manager.opening_probe: Did gaps surface later? Did you have to correct any misunderstandings?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer respond when they're wrong about something? Have you seen that happen?
follow_threads.probe: Did they own it quickly or was it more of a slow acknowledgment? Did it change their behavior?

follow_threads.question: Have you seen evidence of this designer updating their thinking based on new information? Something they used to do or believe that's clearly shifted?
follow_threads.probe: Did they make that change themselves or did someone have to push them?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for ability to learn quickly?

1 means slow to pick up new things or tends to stay in familiar territory. 5 means fast, accurate learner who visibly integrates new knowledge into their work.

competencies.name: Stewards Initiatives and Teams
competencies.what_it_covers: Taking ownership of outcomes beyond individual tasks, caring for team health, and driving initiatives from start to finish.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about an initiative you owned -- not just contributed to, but actually drove. What did owning it look like in practice?
designer.opening_probe: What would have happened to it if you hadn't been driving it? How do you know?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time a project or team dynamic was struggling and you stepped in. What did you do and what was the outcome?
follow_threads.probe: Was it your responsibility to step in or did you choose to? What made you act?

follow_threads.question: How do you think about the health of the team you work with -- not just the work output? Is that part of your job as you see it?
follow_threads.probe: Tell me about a specific thing you've done to care for the team, not just the project.

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for stewarding initiatives and teams?

1 means you're focused primarily on your own tasks and deliverables. 5 means you take genuine ownership of outcomes and team health beyond what's assigned to you, and initiatives you lead reliably succeed.

manager.opening_prompt: Tell me about an initiative this designer has owned. Not just contributed to -- genuinely driven. What did ownership look like?
manager.opening_probe: What would have happened without them? Do you think they know the answer to that?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever stepped in when a project or team dynamic was struggling -- outside of their explicit responsibilities?
follow_threads.probe: Did you ask them to, or did they do it independently? What was the impact?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer think about team health -- not just output? Do they actively contribute to that?
follow_threads.probe: Can you give me a specific example of something they did for the team rather than the project?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for stewarding initiatives and teams?

1 means focused on their own deliverables. 5 means genuine ownership of outcomes and team health well beyond what's assigned to them.

competencies.name: Simplify Complexity
competencies.what_it_covers: Making sense of ambiguous situations, structuring messy information, and communicating clarity to others.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a project where the problem space was genuinely confusing when you came into it. How did you find your footing?
designer.opening_probe: What was the first thing you did to make it less confusing? How did you know when you understood it well enough to start designing?

follow_threads.question: Walk me through a time you had to take a large messy set of information -- research, requirements, stakeholder input -- and turn it into something the team could act on. How did you structure it?
follow_threads.probe: Did anyone push back on how you framed it? Did the structure hold up?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time you had to explain something genuinely complex to someone who didn't have your context. How did you know they actually understood it?
follow_threads.probe: Did you have to change your approach mid-conversation? What gave you the signal to adjust?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for simplifying complexity?

1 means you're still developing your ability to navigate ambiguity and structure messy situations. 5 means you're the person who brings clarity to chaos -- for yourself and for others.

manager.opening_prompt: Think about a time this designer had to work through a genuinely ambiguous or complex situation. How did they approach it?
manager.opening_probe: How much direction did they need from you? Where did they get stuck?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer taken something messy -- competing requirements, sprawling research, conflicting input -- and structured it in a way that helped the team move forward?
follow_threads.probe: Did the team actually use the structure they created, or did it sit there?

follow_threads.question: How effective is this designer at explaining complex things to stakeholders or cross-functional partners without the same context?
follow_threads.probe: Can you think of a time it landed really well, and a time it didn't? What was different?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for simplifying complexity?

1 means still needs support navigating ambiguity. 5 means the person who reliably brings clarity to messy situations for themselves and others.

competencies.name: Inspire with Data
competencies.what_it_covers: Using quantitative and qualitative data to inform, persuade, and build confidence in design decisions.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time you used data -- quantitative or qualitative -- to make a case for a design decision. How did you frame it and did it land?
designer.opening_probe: What data did you use? How did you decide what to emphasize? Did it change anyone's mind?

follow_threads.question: Have you ever been in a situation where the data pointed one way and your design instinct pointed another? What did you do?
follow_threads.probe: How did that tension resolve? Looking back, who was right?

follow_threads.question: How do you use AI to work with data -- pulling insights, identifying patterns, building a story from numbers? Tell me about a specific case.
follow_threads.probe: How did you verify what it surfaced? Was there anything that turned out to be wrong or misleading?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for inspiring with data?

1 means data rarely shows up in how you make or communicate design decisions. 5 means you're fluent in using data to build conviction and move people -- quantitative and qualitative, in service of design.

manager.opening_prompt: Can you point to a time this designer used data effectively to make a case or build conviction around a design decision?
manager.opening_probe: What kind of data did they use? Did it actually change the conversation?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever been wrong because they trusted data that turned out to be misleading or incomplete? What happened?
follow_threads.probe: How did they handle being wrong? Did it change how they use data?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer use AI in their data work? Are they critical about what it surfaces?
follow_threads.probe: Have you seen them present AI-surfaced insights without enough scrutiny?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for inspiring with data?

1 means data rarely features in their design reasoning. 5 means fluent and persuasive use of data to build conviction and move people.

competencies.name: Efficiency & Progress
competencies.what_it_covers: Self-management, prioritization, making smart trade-offs, and unblocking work at the right scope.

designer.opening_prompt: Walk me through how you manage your workload when multiple things are competing for your attention. What's your actual system?
designer.opening_probe: How do you decide what's most important? What falls through the cracks and why?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time a project or decision was stuck and you helped move it forward. What were you waiting on and what did you do?
follow_threads.probe: Did you do it because it was your job, or did you step in because no one else was going to?

follow_threads.question: Has there been a time when moving fast created a problem you had to clean up later? What happened and what would you do differently?
follow_threads.probe: Would you make the same call again? What was the real cost of moving fast?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for efficiency and progress?

1 means you're still developing your ability to manage your own work and keep things moving. 5 means highly self-directed, you unblock others regularly, and make smart deliberate trade-offs.

manager.opening_prompt: How does this designer handle competing priorities? Do they triage independently or come to you for direction?
manager.opening_probe: Have you had to step in because something important wasn't getting attention? How do they signal when they're overloaded?

follow_threads.question: Think about a time this designer helped move something forward that was stuck. What did they do and how much of it was independent versus prompted?
follow_threads.probe: Was the unblocking limited to their own work or did it benefit others?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever moved too fast and created a problem? What happened and how did they handle it?
follow_threads.probe: Did they own it? Did it pattern-repeat?

manager.rating_prompt:

competencies.name: Ships Reliably
competencies.what_it_covers: Consistent follow-through, predictable delivery, and being someone others can count on to get things across the finish line.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a project that was hard to ship -- not because of design difficulty, but because of the surrounding complexity. Dependencies, alignment, competing priorities. How did you get it across the line?
designer.opening_probe: What nearly stopped it? What did you do when it felt like it was going to stall?

follow_threads.question: How do others -- engineers, PMs, stakeholders -- experience working with you toward a deadline? What would they say?
follow_threads.probe: Is there a gap between how you think you show up and how others experience it? What's the gap?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time you had to reset expectations on a timeline or deliverable. How did you handle that conversation?
follow_threads.probe: How early did you flag it? What was the reaction?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for shipping reliably?

1 means delivery is inconsistent or requires a lot of external support to finish things. 5 means others genuinely rely on you to get things across the line and you rarely miss without warning.

manager.opening_prompt: How reliable is this designer when it comes to delivery? Can the team count on them to finish what they start?

follow_threads.question: How do engineers and PMs describe working with this designer toward a deadline? What's the actual experience?
follow_threads.probe: Have you heard feedback -- positive or negative -- from cross-functional partners about their reliability?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever had to reset expectations on a timeline? How did they handle it -- early signal or last minute?
follow_threads.probe: How did the team receive it? Did it affect trust?

manager.rating_prompt:

1 means inconsistent delivery requiring external support. 5 means the team genuinely counts on them and they rarely miss without warning.

competencies.name: Working in the Open
competencies.what_it_covers: Sharing work early, inviting feedback, creating visibility into process, and building trust through transparency.

designer.opening_prompt: How early do you typically share work in progress? What does working in the open look like in your practice?
designer.opening_probe: Tell me about a time sharing early changed the direction of something. What happened?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time sharing unfinished work made you uncomfortable. How did you handle it and what came from it?
follow_threads.probe: What was the risk you were taking? Was it worth it?

follow_threads.question: How do you create visibility into your design process for people who aren't in the room -- engineers, stakeholders, leadership? What's your approach?
follow_threads.probe: Has a lack of visibility on your work ever caused a problem? What happened?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for working in the open?

1 means you tend to work privately until something feels ready. 5 means working in the open is a deliberate practice -- you share early, create visibility, and use feedback as a core part of your process.

manager.opening_prompt: How does this designer share work in progress? Do they work in the open or do they tend to hold work until it's ready?
manager.opening_probe: Has working privately (or too early) ever caused a problem? What happened?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer's transparency about their process -- or lack of it -- affected how others on the team or cross-functional partners experience working with them?
follow_threads.probe: Have you had to encourage them to share earlier or to be more visible about where they are?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time this designer shared something unfinished that led to a better outcome.
follow_threads.probe: Did they do it by instinct or did someone have to push them?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for working in the open?

1 means tends to work privately. 5 means shares early and deliberately, creates visibility, and uses feedback as a core part of how they work.

competencies.name: Advocates for the User
competencies.what_it_covers: Consistently centering user needs in design and cross-functional discussions, and making the case for users when it's inconvenient.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time you advocated for the user in a conversation where it was inconvenient -- where business pressure, timelines, or stakeholder preferences were pointing the other way. What happened?
designer.opening_probe: How did you make the case? Did it change the outcome?

follow_threads.question: How do you stay connected to actual users in your day-to-day work? Not just through research -- what does that look like in practice?
follow_threads.probe: Has something you learned directly from a user recently changed how you thought about a design problem?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a design decision where you had to balance user needs against business or technical constraints. How did you navigate that?
follow_threads.probe: Did you feel like you got it right? What would you do differently?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for advocating for the user?

1 means user advocacy is inconsistent or gets crowded out by other pressures. 5 means you reliably center user needs in your work and conversations, and you make the case for users even when it's inconvenient.

manager.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time this designer advocated for the user in a situation where it was inconvenient or required some courage. What did they do?
manager.opening_probe: Did it change the outcome? How did the team receive it?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer stay connected to actual users? Is it just through formal research or do they have other ways of maintaining that connection?
follow_threads.probe: Has their user knowledge ever surfaced something that others in the room missed?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever let business or technical pressure override user needs in a way you thought was the wrong call?
follow_threads.probe: Did you step in? Did they recognize it themselves later?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for advocating for the user?

1 means user advocacy is inconsistent or gets crowded out. 5 means reliably centers users, makes the case even when inconvenient, and has the team's trust on this.

competencies.name: Influences and Mentors Others
competencies.what_it_covers: Raising the capability of others, sharing knowledge, influencing cross-functionally, and building design credibility beyond the immediate team.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time you helped a more junior designer grow in a meaningful way. What did you actually do and what changed for them?
designer.opening_probe: Did you give them the answer or help them find it? What's the difference in your mind?

follow_threads.question: How do you influence people who don't report to you -- engineers, PMs, other designers, leadership? Tell me about a specific case where you moved someone's thinking.
follow_threads.probe: What made them open to it? What would have closed them off?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time you shaped how your team approaches design -- a practice, a standard, a way of working -- not through authority but through example or persuasion.
follow_threads.probe: Has it stuck? How do you know?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for influencing and mentoring others?

1 means you're primarily focused on your own growth and delivery. 5 means you're actively raising the capability of others around you and your influence extends well beyond your immediate team.

manager.opening_prompt: Tell me about a specific way this designer has raised the capability of someone on the team. What did they do and what changed?
manager.opening_probe: Did they tend to give answers or ask questions? Which is more valuable in your observation?

follow_threads.question: How does this designer influence people outside of direct reporting relationships -- cross-functionally, with leadership, with other designers?
follow_threads.probe: Have you seen them move someone's thinking who wasn't already inclined to agree?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer shaped how your team works -- a practice, a standard, a way of approaching problems -- through example or persuasion rather than authority?
follow_threads.probe: Has it stuck? Would the team keep doing it if this designer left?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for influencing and mentoring others?

1 means focused on their own delivery. 5 means actively raising others' capability and influence extends well beyond the immediate team.

competencies.name: Accelerate Learning
competencies.what_it_covers: Using AI to build knowledge faster, verify what it produces, and close gaps in domain understanding.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about a time you used AI to get up to speed on something you didn't know well -- a market, a user type, a domain, a technology. How did you use it and how did you handle what it gave you?
designer.opening_probe: How did you verify it? Did you find anything wrong or incomplete?

follow_threads.question: Has AI ever given you confidently wrong information that you caught? What happened and how did you catch it?
follow_threads.probe: What would have happened if you'd used it without checking?

follow_threads.question: How has your approach to using AI for learning evolved? What do you do differently now than when you started?
follow_threads.probe: What's a mistake you made early that you wouldn't make now?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for using AI to accelerate learning?

1 means you rarely use AI to build knowledge, or you use it but don't verify what it tells you. 5 means you use AI as a genuine learning accelerant with strong verification habits and clear judgment about where it's reliable.

manager.opening_prompt: Have you seen this designer use AI to get up to speed on something -- a domain, a tool, a type of problem? How did they handle what it gave them?
manager.opening_probe: Did they verify it? Did anything they learned from AI turn out to be wrong?

follow_threads.question: Has this designer ever used AI-sourced information without enough scrutiny and had it cause a problem?
follow_threads.probe: How did they respond when they found out? Did it change their practice?

follow_threads.question: Has their use of AI for learning visibly improved or changed over the time you've worked with them?
follow_threads.probe: What's different now versus when they started?

manager.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've observed, where would you put this designer on a 1 to 5 for using AI to accelerate learning?

1 means rarely uses AI for learning or doesn't verify what it produces. 5 means strong, disciplined use of AI as a learning accelerant with clear judgment about reliability.

competencies.name: Adopt New Workflows
competencies.what_it_covers: Integrating AI into the design process in ways that genuinely improve output quality or leverage, not just speed.

designer.opening_prompt: Tell me about an AI tool or workflow you've adopted in the last year that's actually changed how you work. What's different now?
designer.opening_probe: Did it make you faster, better, or both? Would you have gotten to the same outcome without it?

follow_threads.question: Are there parts of your process where you've deliberately not adopted AI tools? Why?
follow_threads.probe: Has that position shifted over time? What would change your mind?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time an AI workflow that seemed promising didn't actually improve your work. What happened?
follow_threads.probe: How did you figure out it wasn't working? Did you stick with it too long?

designer.rating_prompt:
Based on what you've shared, where would you put yourself on a 1 to 5 for adopting new AI workflows?

1 means you're not actively integrating AI into how you work. 5 means you're thoughtfully and deliberately adopting AI workflows that genuinely improve your leverage, with clear judgment about what's worth adopting and what isn't.

manager.opening_prompt: Has this designer adopted any AI tools or workflows that have genuinely changed how they work? What's different?

follow_threads.question: Does this designer show good judgment about which AI workflows to adopt and which to pass on?

manager.rating_prompt:

1 means not actively integrating AI into their work. 5 means thoughtful, deliberate adoption that genuinely improves their leverage and the quality of their output.

designer.rating_prompt:

manager.opening_prompt: Has this designer used AI to make their work meaningfully better -- not just faster? Can you point to a specific example?

designer.opening_probe: How did you evaluate it? What made you pursue it rather than dismiss it?

follow_threads.question: Tell me about a time you used AI to challenge an assumption you or your team were holding. What happened?

designer.rating_prompt:

1 means AI is primarily a production tool for you -- it helps you execute but doesn't change what you explore. 5 means you actively use AI to expand what's possible, challenge assumptions, and get to ideas you genuinely wouldn't have reached otherwise.
